opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'm probably a bit more skeptical than a lot of people in the AI discourse about very short timelines for automating the whole industrial economy. I want to separate a few things that often get collapsed together.

One question is when we'll have systems that can do a lot of cognitive tasks well: writing code, drafting documents, answering questions, maybe even doing chunks of research. We're clearly making fast progress there. But "automating the existing industrial economy" is a much bigger claim. The economy isn't just a pile of tasks you can benchmark. It's an enormous web of physical infrastructure, tacit knowledge, institutions, supply chains, legal responsibility, and trust between people. A lot of what makes a factory or a hospital or a logistics network actually work is knowledge that was never written down. It lives in the heads of people who've done the job for twenty years, and in the informal norms of how teams coordinate.

So even if you had a model that was, in some abstract sense, as capable as a skilled worker, you'd still face a long, messy diffusion process. You have to integrate it into existing systems, figure out who's accountable when it fails, retool physical plants, and deal with robotics, which is still far behind language models in reliability and cost. Historically, general-purpose technologies like electricity or computing took decades to really reshape productivity, because organizations had to restructure themselves around them.

There's also a technical reason I'm cautious. Current systems are very impressive at pattern completion, but they're still brittle in ways that matter a lot for real-world deployment. They don't robustly model the world, plan reliably over long horizons, or understand what the people they're working with actually want, including all the unstated constraints. In high-stakes settings, that reliability gap is the whole ballgame. Ninety-five percent reliable is fantastic for a chatbot and unacceptable for running a chemical plant.

So my rough view is that we'll see significant automation of particular sectors and task categories over the next five to ten years, especially digital, information-heavy work. Wholesale automation of the industrial economy, in the sense that humans become economically peripheral, looks to me more like a multi-decade process, if it happens at all in that form. And honestly, I think "if it happens at all in that form" is the more important part. Whether we should aim for full automation is a normative question, not just a forecasting one. I'd much rather we build systems that augment human agency and fit into our institutions in ways people can actually endorse than race toward replacing everyone as fast as possible and hope it works out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automation and economic diffusion but does not say that new industries will emerge beyond the existing industrial economy.

r002.rationale: It describes wholesale automation as a “multi-decade process,” without clearly estimating that it is roughly one or two decades away.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest response in Tan Zhi Xuan's voice, drawing on how they tend to think about AI timelines, pluralism, and the gap between benchmark capability and real-world deployment.

Yeah, so I think I'm more skeptical than a lot of people in my immediate intellectual environment about the really short timelines, and I want to be careful to separate a few different things that often get run together when people talk about "automating the economy."

One is the question of whether we'll get systems that can do, in principle, most of the cognitive tasks that make up knowledge work. The second is whether those systems actually get deployed at scale across existing industries. And the third, which is the one your question is really pointing at, is the physical, industrial economy — manufacturing, logistics, construction, agriculture, maintenance, all the stuff that involves atoms rather than bits.

On the first, I think progress has been genuinely fast, and I don't want to downplay that. But I think a lot of the forecasting discourse implicitly assumes that if you can do a task in a benchmark setting, you can do it in the world, and that's just not how it has worked historically. Benchmarks are drawn from a distribution that's been curated to be legible and verifiable. Real jobs involve a lot of tacit knowledge, a lot of context that isn't written down anywhere, a lot of coordination with other people who have their own goals and norms. So there's this long tail of integration work that I think gets systematically underestimated.

On the industrial side specifically, I'd point out that the bottleneck has basically never been intelligence. We've had the cognitive capacity to design better factories for a long time. The bottlenecks are capital, regulation, supply chains, physical robotics that are reliable enough to not break or hurt anyone, and the fact that a lot of industrial knowledge lives in specific people and specific places. Robotics is improving, but the data problem there is very different from language — you don't have the internet's worth of embodied experience lying around. And even once you have a capable robot, the diffusion through the economy happens on the timescale of capital depreciation cycles, which is decades, not months.

So my honest assessment is something like: I think we'll see very substantial automation of narrow, well-specified cognitive tasks within this decade, and that will be economically significant. But "the existing industrial economy" as a whole being automated, in the sense people sometimes mean where you have AI systems running the whole thing end to end — I'd put that much further out, and I'd put a lot of uncertainty on it. And I think part of what shapes that uncertainty is not technical at all. It's about what societies decide they want. Automation isn't just something that happens to us; it's a choice that gets made through institutions, through labor negotiations, through regulation, and I think that's actually a good thing. I'd rather we treat the timeline as something we're collectively determining rather than something we're just forecasting as if it were the weather.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automating existing industries but does not say that new industries will emerge.

r002.rationale: It says automation of the whole existing industrial economy is “much further out” and mentions diffusion taking decades, but gives no estimate of roughly one or two decades.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between AI being able to perform a task and the economy actually reorganizing around that capability. Those can have very different timelines.

For work that happens entirely on a computer, you can imagine fairly rapid changes. But automating the existing industrial economy also means dealing with factories, construction, transportation, maintenance—all these activities where you have to interact reliably with the physical world. Even if the intelligence were available tomorrow, you would still need to build equipment, deploy it, and integrate it into existing processes.

So I’m hesitant to give a single date. A convincing demonstration is very different from a system that operates economically, safely, and reliably across the range of conditions people encounter at work. And automating most tasks doesn’t necessarily eliminate the bottlenecks created by the remaining tasks.

My expectation would be uneven progress: substantial automation in some areas while others remain dependent on people for considerably longer. The question is not just how quickly AI gets better, but how quickly we can turn those improvements into dependable systems throughout the economy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automation across existing sectors but does not say new industries will emerge beyond them.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of one or two decades; it says it is hesitant to give a single date.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate automating particular tasks from automating the entire industrial economy. Those are very different milestones. An AI system might be able to do most of the cognitive work involved in a job, but deploying it reliably requires changes to organizations, infrastructure, and sometimes regulation. And once you get into physical production, you also have to manufacture and deploy the robots and equipment.

So I’m quite uncertain about a single timeline. You could see very rapid progress in capabilities alongside much slower adoption across the economy. The bottleneck might shift from intelligence to things like energy, manufacturing capacity, or coordinating all these changes.

I’d want to look at specific sectors and ask: what actually prevents this process from being automated today? Is it a capability limitation, a reliability limitation, or a deployment cost? That gives you a more useful forecast than extrapolating directly from improvements in AI benchmarks to a date when the whole economy is automated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automating existing sectors and deployment bottlenecks, but does not say that new industries will emerge.

r002.rationale: It gives no one- or two-decade estimate; it explicitly describes the timeline as uncertain.
